About the Planets

Our solar system has eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. There are five officially recognized dwarf planets in our solar system: Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake, and Eris.

8

Planets

5

Dwarf Planets

Introduction

What is a planet? The word traces back to the ancient Greek word planēt, which means “wanderer.” A more modern definition can be found in the Merriam-Webster dictionary, which defines a planet as “any of the large bodies that revolve around the Sun in the solar system.”

In 2006, the International Astronomical Union (IAU) — a group of astronomers that names objects in our solar system — agreed on their own definition of [“planet.”](https://www.iau.org/IAU/Science/What-we-do/Pluto-and-the-Developing-Landscape-of-Our-Solar-System.aspx?WebsiteKey=9e4eaea2-b0d6-4c4b-bd18-913a208b91be#Pluto-4) This new definition  caused Pluto's famous “demotion” to a dwarf planet, and reduced the solar system census from nine planets to eight.

[Learn More: ‘What is a planet?’](https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/planets/what-is-a-planet/)

Saturn's Shapes

NASA’s Hubble Tracks New Decagon Encircling Saturn’s South Pole

Recent observations with NASA’s [Hubble Space Telescope](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/hubble/) have revealed a giant, evolving, 10-sided atmospheric wave encircling Saturn's south pole. This discovery marks the first time a large, regular-sided jet pattern has been observed in the planet's southern hemisphere.  

[Learn about Saturn's Decagon](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/hubble/nasas-hubble-tracks-new-decagon-encircling-saturns-south-pole/)

NASA, ESA, STScI, Agustin Sánchez-Lavega (UPV), Amy Simon (NASA-GSFC), Michael Wong (UC Berkeley); Image Processing: Alyssa Pagan 

Saturn's Hexagon

In Saturn's northern hemisphere, an enormous spinning hexagon in the clouds at its north pole was first spotted in the 1980s. The hurricane-like vortex has an eye about 50 times larger than a typical Earth hurricane, and a maximum wind speed about double that of the strongest cyclones here. 

[Learn about Saturn's Hexagon](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/cassini/science/saturn/hexagon-in-motion/)

NASA/JPL-Caltech/Space Science Institute 

Inner Planets

The first four planets from the Sun are Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars. These inner planets also are known as terrestrial planets because they have solid surfaces. 

Mercury Facts
Mercury is the planet nearest to the Sun, and the smallest planet in our solar system.
[Explore Mercury](https://science.nasa.gov/mercury/facts/)

Venus Facts
Venus is the second planet from the Sun, and the sixth largest planet.
[Explore Venus](https://science.nasa.gov/venus/venus-facts/)

Earth Facts
Earth – our home planet – is the third planet from the Sun, and the fifth largest planet.
[Explore Earth](https://science.nasa.gov/earth/facts/)

Mars Facts
Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun, and the seventh largest planet.
[Explore Mars](https://science.nasa.gov/mars/facts/) 

Outer Planets 

The giant planets in the outer solar system don't have hard surfaces. Instead, they have swirling gases above a core. Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants. Uranus and Neptune are ice giants. 

Jupiter Facts
Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun, and the largest planet in our solar system.
[Explore Jupiter](https://science.nasa.gov/jupiter/facts/)

Saturn Facts
Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun, the second largest planet in our solar system.
[Explore Saturn](https://science.nasa.gov/saturn/facts/)

Uranus Facts
Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun, and the third largest planet in our solar system. 
[Explore Uranus](https://science.nasa.gov/uranus/facts/)

Neptune Facts
Neptune is the eighth and most distant planet in our solar system. It's the fourth largest planet.
[Explore Neptune](https://science.nasa.gov/neptune/facts/) 

Dwarf Planets

Dwarf planets include longtime favorite Pluto, Ceres, Makemake, Haumea, and Eris. Ceres is the only dwarf planet in the inner solar system. It's in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.

Ceres Facts
Dwarf planet Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, and it's the only dwarf planet in the inner solar system.
[Explore Ceres](https://science.nasa.gov/dwarf-planets/ceres/facts/)

Pluto Facts
Pluto was long considered our solar system's ninth planet. It was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 by the International Astronomical Union.
[Explore Pluto](https://science.nasa.gov/dwarf-planets/pluto/facts/)

Haumea Facts
Haumea was nicknamed Santa by one discovery team. It is oval-shaped, and is one of the fastest rotating large objects in our solar system.
[Explore Haumea](https://science.nasa.gov/dwarf-planets/haumea/)

Makemake Facts
Makemake is slightly smaller than Pluto, and is the second-brightest object in the Kuiper Belt, while Pluto is the brightest. 
[Explore Makemake](https://science.nasa.gov/dwarf-planets/makemake/)

Eris Facts
The discovery of Eris helped trigger the debate in the scientific community that led to the decision to clarify the definition of a planet. 
[Explore Eris](https://science.nasa.gov/dwarf-planets/eris/)
